companion.title: Two Coin Tosses and a Stubborn Misconception
companion.subtitle: Independence, ordered outcomes, and why a fair coin is never 'due' for anything

chapters.title: Independence and the Memoryless Coin
chapters.goal: Understand why past tosses do not change the probability of the next toss.

claims.text: An ideal fair coin gives heads and tails each a probability of one half on any single toss.
claims.reason: cue-1 states heads and tails each have probability one half on a toss.

claims.text: Independence means knowing one toss's result does not alter the probability distribution of the next toss.
claims.reason: cue-1 defines independence exactly this way.

claims.text: After three heads in a row, the probability of tails on the next toss remains one half because the coin has no memory.
claims.reason: cue-2 states tails remains one half and the coin has no memory.

claims.text: The belief that tails becomes 'due' after a streak of heads is identified as a mistake for an independent fair coin.
claims.reason: cue-2 labels the 'tails is due' belief a mistake for the independent fair coin; cue-1 gives the independence context.

checks.concept: Independence: streaks do not change the next-toss probability
checks.question: A fair coin, tossed independently, has landed heads three times in a row. What is the probability of tails on the next toss?

choices.text: Greater than one half, since tails is now due
choices.explanation: This is the misconception the source addresses; the coin has no memory, so streaks do not raise the chance of tails.
Correct: independence means earlier results do not change the next toss's distribution, so tails stays at one half.

choices.text: Less than one half, since heads is on a streak
choices.explanation: This assumes a 'hot' coin, but independence rules out any influence of past tosses on the next one.

recovery.question: For independent fair tosses, which statement best describes how the result of one toss affects the next?

choices.text: It does not change the probability distribution for the next toss
It makes the opposite outcome more likely on the next toss
It makes the same outcome more likely on the next toss

recovery.explanation: Independence is defined as knowing one toss's outcome not changing the next toss's distribution; the coin has no memory.

chapters.title: Counting Ordered Outcomes for Two Tosses
chapters.goal: List the four ordered outcomes and compute probabilities for 'exactly one head' and 'at least one head'.

claims.text: Two independent fair tosses have four ordered outcomes—HH, HT, TH, TT—each with probability one quarter.
claims.reason: cue-3 lists the four ordered outcomes each with probability one quarter.

claims.text: Order matters when listing elementary outcomes, so HT and TH are distinct.
claims.reason: cue-3 states order matters; cue-4 treats HT and TH as two distinct outcomes.

claims.text: Exactly one head has probability one half because it arises from two distinct outcomes, HT and TH.
claims.reason: cue-4 states exactly one head arises from HT or TH with probability one half.

claims.text: Counting only one of HT or TH would miss half of the favorable outcomes for exactly one head, while two heads has probability one quarter.
claims.reason: cue-4 states counting only one would miss half of favorable outcomes and two heads has probability one quarter.

claims.text: At least one head has probability three quarters, computed either by adding HH, HT, TH or by subtracting the probability of TT from one.
claims.reason: cue-5 gives three quarters and both the direct count and the subtract-from-one method.

checks.concept: Probability of exactly one head in two tosses via ordered outcomes
checks.question: For two independent fair tosses, what is the probability of exactly one head?

choices.explanation: This counts only one of HT or TH, missing half of the favorable outcomes.
Correct: HT and TH are two distinct outcomes, each one quarter, totaling one half.
This is the probability of at least one head, which also includes HH.

recovery.question: Which ordered outcomes of two fair tosses make up the event 'exactly one head'?
recovery.explanation: Exactly one head occurs as HT or TH; both are distinct ordered outcomes, giving probability one half.

chapters.title: Models Versus Small Samples
chapters.goal: Recognize that a probability model states assumptions, not guarantees about small batches.

claims.text: A probability model describes assumptions rather than guaranteeing that every small batch matches expected proportions.
claims.reason: cue-6 states a model describes assumptions, not a guarantee about small batches.

claims.text: Four tosses do not have to contain exactly two heads.
claims.reason: cue-6 states four tosses do not have to contain exactly two heads.

claims.text: If the coin is biased or tosses are dependent, the fair independent model must be reconsidered.
claims.reason: cue-6 states this condition for reconsidering the model.

checks.concept: A probability model does not guarantee small-batch proportions
checks.question: A fair coin is tossed four times. According to the source, which is true?

choices.text: It must show exactly two heads
choices.explanation: The source says four tosses do not have to contain exactly two heads; the model is not a guarantee.

choices.text: It need not show exactly two heads, since the model states assumptions, not guarantees
choices.explanation: Correct: a model describes assumptions, and small batches can deviate from expected proportions.

choices.text: Any deviation from two heads proves the coin is biased
choices.explanation: Deviation alone is expected in small batches; bias or dependence are reasons to reconsider the model, not proven by one batch.

recovery.question: What does a probability model, as described in the source, actually provide?

choices.text: A guarantee that each small batch matches expected proportions
A description of assumptions about the process
A rule that streaks must even out within a few tosses

recovery.explanation: The model describes assumptions; it does not guarantee small-batch proportions, and streaks do not have to even out.

An elementary result of two tosses where order matters, such as HT versus TH, each with probability one quarter.
